purpose: The colour every declared guard is expected to be, and — for the ones expected to be red — who owns that red, why it is there, and what would close it. Read ci/check_open_reds.py for the argument; the short form is that an accepted red and a new red must not look the same, and before this file the only record of an acceptance was a number somebody remembered.
how_to_add_an_entry: An entry with expect=red is a LEASE, not a grant. It needs an owner who can actually close it, a `closes_when` that names the observable event, a `signature` that is the exact red being accepted (not a wildcard), and a `review_by` after which the lane fails until somebody re-reads it. If you cannot write `closes_when`, you do not have an accepted red, you have an unowned one, and the honest thing is to leave the lane failing. It also needs an `extent`: `signature` is a SUBSTRING test and a substring cannot notice a second subject joining an accepted red (Switch, 2026-08-03), so an entry must name the MEMBERS its acceptance is granted over. Growing the set is `extent_widened`; shrinking it is `extent_narrowed`, which is good news and must be re-read rather than left to cover something in principle.
how_to_remove_an_entry: DO NOT DELETE IT. Set `expect` to "green" and leave it running: that is what turns the next regression in that check into an unaccounted_red instead of a silence. The screen tells you when: an expect=red entry whose check has gone green is FAIL(condition=stale_acceptance). Deleting an entry outright removes the CHECK from the register, not just the acceptance, and on 2026-08-03 that is exactly what happened -- three entries were deleted, the denominator went from 8 to 5, and the screen printed PASS with a red check in the tree it had stopped looking at. If a subject really should stop being watched, move its id to `retired` with an owner, a date and a reason; `subjects` is append-only and every name in it must be in one list or the other.

That is the same incommensurable-sum defect as the '48 failures' headline I carried for three sessions — 42 ledger + 4 instrument + 2 residual, three different kinds of thing behind one number. An entry for the sum would accept all five as one red and go on accepting a sixth. This screen runs host-free, so it cannot observe that check's colour, and a colour this screen cannot observe must not be declared here — UNOBSERVABLE is not green, and an entry that is satisfied by a skip is an acceptance granted by an absence. not_declared_here.gen_proof_ledger.py --check discards its: The same run computes the note that would explain itself and then does not print it. `check_against_build` returns (failures, notes) and appends a note naming the toolchain difference whenever the build's toolchain differs from the entries'; `cmd_check` prints notes ONLY after the PASS line and returns 1 from the failure branch before reaching them (gen_proof_ledger.py:1088-1100 vs :1105). On PASS, where nothing needs explaining, the notes are printed in full. That is the session's shape one more time: the explanation exists, is computed, and reaches nobody. Verified by grepping a live Linux --check run for 'toolchain' -- zero hits, in a run where all 103 failures have a toolchain cause. Owner: mouse. One-line repair: move the `for n in notes` loop above the `if build_failures:` block.

known_limits.limit: check_artifact_frame.py asks 'has the source this reading is ABOUT moved since the reading was taken', and 'is ABOUT' is a list the writer typed into the frame. An artifact can therefore still be stale with respect to a fix in a path nobody named, and the screen will say PASS. The cheap form makes the common case detectable; it does not make the general case impossible.
known_limits.closes_when: Either (a) a claims register lands — each claim naming its evidence — in which case subject_paths is DERIVED rather than declared and this limit is gone, or (b) a real stale citation gets through a declared subject_paths list, which would be the evidence that the cheap form is not enough and the strong form is worth building. Until one of those happens the honest state is 'known, bounded, not worth the build'.

known_limits.limit: The census walks every revision that touched evidence/proof_ledger.jsonl. In a shallow clone most of those revisions are not present, so the walk is short and the screen would have reported PASS over history it cannot see — the exact defect it exists to catch, arriving through the checkout rather than through a merge. I declared this in prose in session 18 and did not guard it. It is now GUARDED — history_is_complete() reports ERROR(instrument=truncated_history) and exits 2 — but a guard is not a fix: in a shallow CI checkout the census still rules on nothing, and a lane that only tests for exit 1 would read that as tolerable.
known_limits.closes_when: The workflow that runs ci/check_ledger_census.py declares fetch-depth 0 (or its equivalent) AND a lane test asserts that exit 2 fails the lane. Then the guard becomes unreachable in CI rather than merely loud, and this entry is retired with owner, date and reason like any other.
